what: Haemonetics makes equipment used with blood. Its machines collect plasma from donors, salvage and return a patient’s own blood during surgery, and its devices and software support hospital transfusion and vascular procedures, including catheters used in heart and vein treatments.
customers: Plasma collection companies running donation centres, hospitals performing surgery and managing blood supply, and interventional cardiologists and vascular specialists.
money: Equipment and disposables used to collect plasma in donation centres.
Blood salvage during surgery, haemostasis testing and vascular closure and catheter devices.
Equipment for blood banks collecting and processing whole blood and platelets.
moat: The machines are sold or placed with customers and then consume single-use disposables with every procedure, which produces recurring revenue for the machine’s life. In plasma collection in particular, Haemonetics equipment is installed across a large share of the world’s donation centres, and switching would mean retraining staff and revalidating a regulated process.
risks: Revenue declined from $1.4B in 2025 to $1.3B in 2026, which for a company priced at 53.3 times earnings is the central concern.
The largest plasma collection customers have been consolidating and insourcing equipment decisions, which pressures pricing.
The shares trade at about 22.2 times EV/EBITDA and 18.4 times free cash flow, a full price given the revenue direction.
Debt of $1.3B against $245.4M of cash is meaningful, much of it from acquisitions in the hospital segment.
Reported net income of $103.9M on $1.4B of revenue is a 7.3% margin, low for a medical device company with this installed base.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $298.2M on $1.4B of revenue is strong and far better than the reported earnings suggest.
Disposables consumed with every procedure produce recurring revenue tied to activity rather than to equipment sales.
The hospital segment, particularly vascular and catheter devices, is growing and carries better margins than plasma equipment.
Plasma demand grows steadily because the therapies made from it treat chronic conditions requiring lifelong treatment.
Eleven analysts average a $147.18 target, about 22% above the current price.
watch: Revenue by segment, particularly whether hospital growth is offsetting plasma weakness. The two halves are moving in different directions and the consolidated figure hides it.
view: Haemonetics has the business model medical device investors look for: place a machine with a customer, then sell the single-use disposables consumed with every procedure for as long as the machine runs. Revenue follows activity rather than equipment purchases, and the installed base is sticky because switching means retraining staff and revalidating a regulated process. Across plasma collection centres worldwide, that installed base is substantial.

The problem is who the plasma customers are. A handful of very large companies run most of the world’s plasma collection, they have been consolidating, and they are entirely capable of designing or sourcing their own equipment. When your installed base sits with three or four buyers who know exactly what the machines cost to make, the pricing conversation goes badly over time. That dynamic, rather than any failure of execution, is why plasma revenue has been under pressure.

Management’s response has been to build the hospital segment, which now exceeds plasma and carries better margins — blood salvage during surgery, haemostasis testing, and vascular closure and catheter devices sold to interventional cardiologists. Those customers are thousands of hospitals rather than four plasma companies, which is a structurally stronger position. The acquisitions that built it explain the $1.3 billion of debt.

What makes the stock difficult is that revenue has declined — $1.4 billion to $1.3 billion — while the shares trade at 53.3 times earnings and 22.2 times EV/EBITDA. Free cash flow of $298 million at 18.4 times is the honest measure and still a full price for a business shrinking at the top line. The entire question is whether hospital growth outpaces plasma pressure, and the consolidated revenue figure actively obscures that. The segment detail is where the answer is, and at this multiple I would want to see it before committing.
bull: The hospital segment’s vascular and surgical devices grow faster than plasma declines, shifting the mix toward thousands of hospital customers and better margins.
bear: Consolidated plasma customers keep squeezing equipment pricing, hospital growth cannot offset it, and 53 times earnings on declining revenue corrects.
